question: Three hours after undergoing left hip arthroplasty for chronic hip pain, a 62-year-old man complains of a prickling sensation in his left anteromedial thigh and lower leg. He has never had these symptoms before. He has hyperlipidemia and coronary artery disease. He has had recent right-sided gluteal and thigh pain with ambulation. Vital signs are within normal limits. Sensation to pinprick and light touch are decreased on the anteromedial left thigh as well as medial lower leg. Neurologic exam shows left leg strength 3/5 on hip flexion and 2/5 on knee extension. Patellar reflex is decreased on the left. The remainder of neurologic exam is normal. Dorsalis pedis, popliteal, and femoral pulses are 2+ bilaterally. The surgical incision is without erythema or drainage. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Chronic hip pain -> left hip arthroplasty -> postoperative complications -> 70% CHAIN: Left hip arthroplasty -> potential nerve injury -> 60% CHAIN: Prickling sensation in left anteromedial thigh and lower leg -> sensory nerve involvement -> nerve injury -> 70% CHAIN: Decreased sensation to pinprick and light touch -> sensory nerve dysfunction -> nerve injury -> 80% CHAIN: Left leg weakness on hip flexion and knee extension -> motor nerve involvement -> nerve injury -> 80% CHAIN: Decreased patellar reflex on the left -> nerve injury affecting reflex arc -> 70% CHAIN: Normal pulses in dorsalis pedis, popliteal, and femoral arteries -> unlikely vascular cause -> 90% CHAIN: Symptoms localized to left anteromedial thigh and lower leg -> specific nerve distribution -> nerve injury -> 80% CHAIN: Overall clinical presentation -> consistent with femoral nerve injury -> opb. Femoral nerve injury -> 70%
enhanced_information: The most likely underlying cause of the patient's symptoms is a femoral nerve injury. The clinical presentation, including sensory and motor deficits localized to the left anteromedial thigh and lower leg, along with decreased patellar reflex, is consistent with femoral nerve involvement. The absence of vascular compromise and the specific nerve distribution support this conclusion.
analysis: The patient's symptoms of sensory and motor deficits localized to the left anteromedial thigh and lower leg, along with decreased patellar reflex, are indicative of femoral nerve involvement. The absence of vascular compromise and the specific nerve distribution support this conclusion. Given the clinical presentation and enhanced information provided, a femoral nerve injury is the most likely underlying cause of the patient's symptoms.
